topic: The Hidden Mirror: Planar Graph Duality and Euler's Formula
target_audience: Undergraduate students in Computer Science or Discrete Mathematics

outline.topic: The Hidden Mirror: Planar Graph Duality and Euler's Formula
outline.target_audience: Undergraduate students in Computer Science or Discrete Mathematics

sections.title: Prerequisite: Defining the Planar World
sections.content: Establish the foundation by defining a Planar Graph: a graph that can be drawn in a 2D plane such that no edges cross. Introduce the three fundamental elements: Vertices (V), Edges (E), and Faces (F). Crucially, explain that the 'outer' region surrounding the graph counts as one face.
sections.example: Visualizing a 'Spider's Web' anchored to three trees. The trees are Vertices, the silk threads are Edges, and the gaps between threads (including the vast forest outside) are Faces.

sections.title: The Golden Rule: Euler's Characteristic Formula
sections.content: Introduce the formula V - E + F = 2. Explain that this is a topological invariant for any connected planar graph. This formula acts as the 'balance' that dictates how many faces must exist given a set of vertices and edges. Show a quick animation of adding an edge and seeing how it simultaneously creates a new face, keeping the sum constant.
sections.example: A simple triangle graph: V=3, E=3, F=2 (inner triangle + outer space). Calculation: 3 - 3 + 2 = 2. If we add a tail (a new vertex and edge), V=4, E=4, F=2. Calculation: 4 - 4 + 2 = 2.

sections.title: The Transformation: Constructing the Dual Graph
sections.content: Step-by-step guide to 'Dualization'. 1. Place a new vertex (Dual Vertex) in the center of every face of the original graph G. 2. For every edge in G that separates two faces, draw a new edge (Dual Edge) connecting the corresponding Dual Vertices. This creates a new graph, G*.
sections.example: Imagine a 'Map of Island Kingdoms'. Each kingdom is a Face. We place a 'Capital City' (Dual Vertex) in each kingdom. If two kingdoms share a border (Edge), we build a 'Bridge' (Dual Edge) between their capitals.

sections.title: The Symmetry of Elements
sections.content: Analyze the relationship between the original graph G and its dual G*. Highlight the mathematical 'Mirroring': The number of Vertices in G* equals the number of Faces in G (V* = F). The number of Faces in G* equals the number of Vertices in G (F* = V). The number of Edges remains the same (E* = E). Note that Euler's formula holds perfectly for both.
sections.example: A Cube graph projected on a plane. It has V=8, E=12, F=6. Its dual is an Octahedron, which has V=6, E=12, F=8. They are perfect geometric reflections of one another's properties.

sections.title: Advanced Insight: The Self-Dual Mystery and Application
sections.content: Conclude with the concept of self-duality (graphs that look the same after transformation) and why this matters. Mention applications in electrical circuit design (converting mesh currents to node voltages) and navigation algorithms.
sections.example: The 'Pyramid' (Tetrahedron) example. A pyramid graph has 4 vertices and 4 faces. Its dual also has 4 vertices and 4 faces. Like a shape-shifting robot, it transforms into itself!

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: Defining the Planar World
lecture_lines: A planar graph is drawn without crossing edges.
It consists of vertices, edges, and faces.
Every graph has one infinite outer face.
animations: Highlight the first lecture line in #FFFF00. Show a graph with crossing edges in #FF8C00, then smoothly move a vertex so edges no longer cross.
Highlight the second lecture line in #FFFF00. Individually flash vertices in #FFFFFF, edges in #FFFFFF, and internal regions (faces) in #FF8C00.
Highlight the third lecture line in #FFFF00. Pulse the entire area outside the graph with a faint #FF8C00 glow to identify the infinite outer face.

storyboard.title: The Golden Rule: Euler's Characteristic Formula
lecture_lines: Euler's formula states V minus E plus F equals 2.
This balance holds for all connected planar graphs.
Adding a tail vertex keeps the sum constant.
Adding an edge creates exactly one new face.
The formula remains invariant during these transformations.
animations: Highlight the first lecture line in #FFFF00. Display 'V - E + F = 2' in large #FFFFFF text at the top center.
Highlight the second lecture line in #FFFF00. Create a triangle graph with one attached 'tail' edge in #FF8C00. Label V=4, E=4, F=2 near the graph.
Highlight the third lecture line in #FFFF00. Add a new vertex and edge to the tail. Update count to V=5, E=5, F=2 and show '5 - 5 + 2 = 2'.
Highlight the fourth lecture line in #FFFF00. Add an edge between two existing vertices to form a new cycle. Update count to V=5, E=6, F=3 and show '5 - 6 + 3 = 2'.
Highlight the fifth lecture line in #FFFF00. Flash the '= 2' part of the formula in #FFFF00 while the graph components pulse in #FF8C00.

storyboard.title: The Transformation: Constructing the Dual Graph
lecture_lines: Every face in G becomes a dual vertex.
Dual vertices connect across shared edge boundaries.
This process builds the dual graph G-star.
animations: Highlight the first lecture line in #FFFF00. Take a planar graph in #FF8C00 and place a #00FFFF dot (dual vertex) in every face, including the exterior.
Highlight the second lecture line in #FFFF00. Draw #00FFFF dashed lines (dual edges) crossing each edge of the #FF8C00 graph to connect the dots.
Highlight the third lecture line in #FFFF00. Fade out the #FF8C00 graph, leaving only the #00FFFF dots and dashed lines, then solidify the dashed lines.

storyboard.title: The Symmetry of Elements
lecture_lines: G and G-star share a deep mathematical symmetry.
Vertices in G-star equal the faces in G.
Faces in G-star equal the vertices in G.
The number of edges remains exactly the same.
Euler's formula holds perfectly for both reflections.
animations: Highlight the first lecture line in #FFFF00. Display a graph G in #FF8C00 and its dual G* in #00FFFF side-by-side.
Highlight the second lecture line in #FFFF00. Flash faces of G in #FF8C00 and then flash corresponding vertices of G* in #00FFFF.
Highlight the third lecture line in #FFFF00. Flash vertices of G in #FF8C00 and then flash corresponding faces of G* in #00FFFF.
Highlight the fourth lecture line in #FFFF00. Simultaneously highlight one edge in G and its crossing edge in G* for all edges to show 1-to-1 correspondence.
Highlight the fifth lecture line in #FFFF00. Show V-E+F=2 for G and V*-E*+F*=2 for G* in #FFFFFF, highlighting how the numbers swap but the sum is invariant.

storyboard.title: Advanced Insight: The Self-Dual Mystery and Application
lecture_lines: Self-dual graphs transform back into themselves.
The tetrahedron is a classic self-dual example.
Duality aids in circuit design and navigation.
animations: Highlight the first lecture line in #FFFF00. Morph a graph G into G* where G* has the exact same structure/layout as G.
Highlight the second lecture line in #FFFF00. Draw a 2D planar projection of a tetrahedron in #FF8C00 and construct its dual in #00FFFF to show they are isomorphic.
Highlight the third lecture line in #FFFF00. Transform the graph into a simplified circuit schematic with vertices as nodes and edges as components, pulsing in #FFFFFF.

issues.description:
[section_1] Implement Manim code for 'Prerequisite: Defining the Planar World'. 
1. Use the finalized storyboard: highlights for crossing edges, vertices, edges, and faces (internal and external). 
2. Follow the lecture lines for timing. 
3. Visuals: Use #FF8C00 for graph elements and #00FFFF for dual-related elements if applicable, but here follow the flash colors (#FFFFFF, #FF8C00) in the storyboard. 
4. Grid: Ensure mobjects and labels do not overlap (B001) and keep the lecture text area clear.

[section_2] Implement Manim code for 'The Golden Rule: Euler\'s Characteristic Formula'.
1. Show 'V - E + F = 2' at top center.
2. Animate a triangle graph with a tail, then add a vertex/edge, then an edge to form a cycle.
3. Update counts (V, E, F) and formula check dynamically.
4. Layout: Avoid stacking complex mobjects vertically (B019) and keep formulas away from axis tips/congested areas (B038).

[section_3] Implement Manim code for 'The Transformation: Constructing the Dual Graph'.
1. Construct the dual graph G* step-by-step: dots in faces (including exterior), dashed lines crossing edges.
2. Finalize by fading G and solidifying G*.
3. Colors: G in #FF8C00, G* in #00FFFF.
4. Clearances: Ensure dual vertices and labels do not collide with original graph edges (B001, B009).

[section_4] Implement Manim code for 'The Symmetry of Elements'.
1. Side-by-side comparison of G (#FF8C00) and G* (#00FFFF).
2. Highlight 1-to-1 correspondences: G faces to G* vertices, G vertices to G* faces, G edges to G* edges.
3. Display Euler's formula for both.
4. Constraint: Limit trajectories or extensions to prevent overlapping with lecture text (B060).

[section_5] Implement Manim code for 'Advanced Insight: The Self-Dual Mystery and Application'.
1. Morph G into G* for a self-dual graph.
2. Show the tetrahedron example (2D planar projection).
3. Transform to circuit schematic.
4. Maintain visual corridor during high-motion morphing (B009).
